cusp

KUSP -- one syllable; starts like 'cup' and ends with the -sp sound of 'wasp.' · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Cusp is a transition point between two states of being.

The orchard stands on the cusp of autumn, its green leaves just beginning to turn.

Example

For two years the three founders have coded in a garage, living on instant noodles. Tonight, for the first time, the demo runs without a single crash -- and with their first real investor pitch tomorrow morning, the startup stands on the cusp of something much bigger.

A cusp is the exact transition point between two states -- struggling experiment on one side, real company on the other. It is the edge where one condition ends and the next begins, and the word almost always travels in the phrase 'on the cusp of.'

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

threshold: A threshold is the entry point you cross into something new -- step over it and you are inside. A cusp is the border itself: on the cusp of adulthood you belong to both childhood and adult life, and to neither, because the crossing has not quite happened.

juncture: A juncture is a critical moment where paths meet and a choice must be made, at any point along the way. A cusp is specifically the edge between two whole states of being -- childhood and adulthood, summer and autumn -- where one condition ends and the next begins.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

middle: the stretch far from any turning point

interior: the inside, away from the edge

Where it sits · how dramatic the coming change feels — verge → cusp → brink

verge vs. cusp: Verge is the calmest and least dramatic of the three -- being on the verge of tears simply says something is about to happen, while standing on the cusp of adulthood already feels like one whole life ending and another beginning.

brink vs. cusp: Brink is the strongest and most dramatic: you stand on the cusp of adulthood but on the brink of disaster -- brink leans toward cliff edges and points of no return.

Build the Word

The pieces

root — cusp-

root — cusp-: point, pointed tip (Latin cuspis 'spear point')

Put it together

Put it together: Cusp comes from Latin cuspis, a spear point. Astronomers used it for the sharp horns of the crescent moon, dentists for the points of a tooth -- and everyday English kept the geometry: a cusp is the single sharp point where two curves, two seasons, or two stages of life meet.

Use the root in a new word: bicuspid

Use the root in a new word: bicuspid: Dentists call the two-pointed tooth just behind your canines a bicuspid.

Root Check

Word Choice

Cusp lives almost entirely inside one phrase: On the cusp of something -- adulthood, fame, a breakthrough, a new season. Learn it as that chunk. The 'of' names the state being entered, and the word always implies the change has not quite happened yet: on the cusp, you belong to both sides and to neither.
